title: EU targets advanced materials leadership by 2035
html:
The European Commission has unveiled a new initiative aimed at making the EU a global leader in the development, production and deployment of advanced materials by 2035. The Advanced Materials for Europe agenda sets ambitious targets for investment, startups and industrial adoption, with a focus on accelerating the transition from laboratory research to commercial production.

The initiative could have significant implications for Europe’s semiconductor, electronics, AI and quantum computing industries, where advanced materials are increasingly critical to performance, efficiency and competitiveness. It also aims to strengthen European supply chains and reduce dependence on technologies and materials developed outside the EU.

EU sets advanced materials targets for 2035

The Commission has proposed three key benchmarks to be achieved by 2035: a 20% increase in research and innovation investment, 20% more EU-based startups and scaleups, and 20% of projects reaching higher deployment levels in safer and more sustainable advanced materials.

Europe already has more than 15,000 companies working in advanced materials, supporting approximately 1.5 million jobs. However, the Commission believes that fragmented investment, limited testing infrastructure and lengthy commercialization processes are holding back the sector.

“Advanced materials will be at the heart of Europe’s next industrial age. They are key to our clean transition, our economic security and our global competitiveness. With this initiative, we are helping Europe turn scientific excellence into industrial leadership, so that innovative materials created in Europe are also produced, scaled up and used in Europe,” said European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.

AI and digitalization to accelerate development

The initiative identifies five priorities for action by 2030, including targeted R&D investment, greater use of AI and digital technologies, improved testing and qualification infrastructure, industrial scale-up support and workforce development.

AI-driven materials discovery is expected to play an important role in shortening development cycles, particularly for applications in next-generation semiconductors, batteries, renewable energy systems and aerospace.

The Commission also wants to improve access to pilot production facilities and introduce demand-side measures, including strategic projects and public procurement, to help innovative materials reach commercial markets.

Council approval and next steps

The proposal builds on the Commission’s 2024 Advanced Materials for Industrial Leadership strategy and complements broader EU efforts to strengthen technological sovereignty and economic security.

The EU has already committed €2.3 billion to advanced materials research under Horizon Europe for 2021–2027, alongside initiatives such as the Innovative Advanced Materials for Europe partnership and the European Advanced Materials Academy.

The proposal must now be adopted by the Council of the EU. Progress will be monitored by the Technology Council for Advanced Materials, with an initial assessment planned for the end of 2028 and a full implementation report due by the end of 2030.
